detail.abstract: A financial service can become easier to enter and harder to put right. Drawing on capability theory, public law and the economics of queues, this article examines remedial congestion as a constraint on the value of financial inclusion. A stationary model identifies conditions under which further expansion reduces marginal user benefit despite continuing gains from the service already provided. Extending the analysis to unreported injuries shows why reduced complaint traffic can conceal continuing harm, and why wider access to redress may require additional processing capacity. Further extensions address growing capacity, changes in the user population, clustered failures and linked stages of correction. Nepal supplies a conceptual and regulatory application, with official financial reports establishing the setting and an uncalibrated model generating propositions for future empirical investigation. The sandbox guidelines' permission to relax some support arrangements, subject to preserving consumer protection, makes effective correction a concrete regulatory question. Expansion decisions should account for the remedial workload imposed on all users of shared processes, including people outside an experiment. Independent incident ascertainment and variation across processing pools would permit that proposition to be tested. The developmental question is how long people must bear an institution's mistakes before their claims become usable again.

detail.abstract: In highly competitive retail environments, customer satisfaction has emerged as a critical determinant of long-term organizational success. As product differentiation becomes increasingly challenging, retailers are compelled to focus on delivering superior value through both tangible and intangible elements of the retail experience. This study examines the interplay between product quality and service quality and their joint influence on customer satisfaction within retail contexts. Drawing on established perspectives in marketing and consumer behavior, the paper conceptualizes product quality and service quality as multidimensional constructs that shape customer evaluations through both functional and experiential mechanisms. Rather than treating these dimensions as independent antecedents, the study emphasizes their complementary and, in certain contexts, compensatory effects in the formation of customer satisfaction. The analysis highlights that high product quality serves as a foundational driver of satisfaction through performance confirmation and perceived value, while service quality enhances emotional responses, facilitates relationship building, and plays a crucial role in service recovery situations. Furthermore, the relative importance of product and service quality is shown to vary across retail formats, levels of customer involvement, and contextual conditions. By adopting an integrated perspective, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of value creation in retail environments. The findings offer important theoretical implications by advancing interaction-based models of customer satisfaction and provide practical insights for retail managers seeking to align product excellence with consistent and high-quality service delivery to achieve sustainable competitive advantage.

detail.abstract: This study examined the competitive effects of Licensed Mobile Money Operators (LMMOs) on commercial bank deposit mobilization and lending spreads in Nigeria from 2019 to 2024. Using a post-positivist mixed-methods design, the empirical strategy combined structural and nonstructural competition metrics including Lerner Index estimation, panel vector autoregression (PVAR), and Difference-inDifferences (DiD) applied to a balanced panel of 22 commercial banks across 24 quarterly observations (N = 528). Findings demonstrate that LMMOs have emerged as a distinct competitive force in Nigeria's retail banking landscape. Mobile money expansion significantly enhanced financial inclusion, reduced bank lending spreads, and eroded commercial banks' pricing power in low-value deposit and payment clearing services. However, competitive impacts were heterogeneous across bank tiers: Tier-3 banks experienced disproportionate margin compression, whereas Tier-1 institutions maintained structural resilience due to their dominance in corporate credit, wholesale banking, and foreign exchange markets. Econometrically, PVAR variance decomposition revealed that LMMO competitive shocks accounted for 18.3% of the variance in commercial bank deposit mobilization and 12.7% of the variance in lending spreads. This confirmed that while LMMOs disrupt retail cash flows, asymmetric regulations specifically credit restrictions on Payment Service Banks (PSBs) preserve banks' foundational role in credit intermediation. The study recommended that the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) should consider phased micro-credit licensing for PSBs alongside enhanced data reporting, while commercial banks accelerate digital transformation and strategic co-opetition with fintech entities.

detail.abstract: This article advances a law-and-economics reframing of standard-essential patent (SEP) licensing, arguing that persistent regulatory and doctrinal confusion stems from analysing SEP licensing as an ordinary, decentralised market transaction governed by substitutability, exit and price competition. It argues instead that SEP licensing is better understood as the performance and completion of an inherently incomplete contractual framework: the "grand bargain" through which SEP holders undertake, as a condition of standard inclusion, to license on fair, reasonable and nondiscriminatory (FRAND) terms, while implementers rely on that commitment to make sunk investments in standard-compliant products. Because the FRAND commitment cannot specify royalties, portfolio allocation or downstream valuation ex ante, bilateral licensing, patent pools, licensing negotiation groups (LNGs) and judicial FRAND determinations are best understood as complementary mechanisms for completing the same underlying bargain, rather than as distinct antitrust phenomena. Applying this contractual paradigm, the article reexamines the competition law treatment of LNGs, arguing that they are more properly analogised to patent pools than to buyer cartels, and reconciles the apparently divergent English and German/Unified Patent Court approaches to SEP adjudication as different institutional methods for supervising performance of the same FRAND undertaking. The analysis has direct implications for the calibrated application of Articles 101 and 102 TFEU to standardisation, collective licensing and post-standardisation opportunism.

title: AI Protecting the Conditions of Virtue - A Self-Screening Constitution for Artificial Systems, and Why It Cannot Make Anyone Good

detail.title: AI Protecting the Conditions of Virtue - A Self-Screening Constitution for Artificial Systems, and Why It Cannot Make Anyone Good

declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: not applicable

detail.abstract:
The problem. Every document that governs how an artificial system behaves contains rules that can point in opposite directions. Be maximally helpful and refuse harmful requests. Prevent imminent harm and protect a third party’s privacy. These are not drafting errors; a document containing no such pairs would be trivial or silent about everything that matters. The question nobody asks of these documents is what happens when two of their own rules collide — whether the text says which prevails.

Why it matters. The conflicts are resolved anyway, because a deployed system meets them and does something. Where the text does not determine the outcome, something else does: a rater’s preference during training, a labelling instruction, an engineering decision nobody recorded. To the extent that a charter fails to adjudicate its own collisions, the operative constitution is not the charter.

What has been established. A screen of the most explicit charter available found a rule of recognition and no rule of adjudication: it settles every question of the form whose instruction prevails and almost none of the form which commitment prevails. Supplying the missing rule by ranking provisions in advance then failed three times, in ways that were measured rather than argued: the natural criterion requires an unavailable measurement, its substitute proved unstable under contested coding, and a formal limit bounds what any provision-level ordering can reach.

What this paper does. It sets out the architecture that survives those failures, drafts a sixty-one article charter to it, screens that charter against its own screening provision before publication, and reports the result. It then asks a question the formal machinery makes urgent: whether a document constrained by rankability can protect individual freedom and the human virtues, or whether the machinery crowds them out.

The answer divides. Freedom as liberty was already protected; freedom as self-direction was not, and eleven new articles supply it at the same drafting discipline — non-substitution of the person’s deliberation, non-cultivation of reliance, disclosure of the unaided path, non-flattery, and a duty to voice disagreement held. The virtues are not protected and cannot be, because a provision undertaking to produce them would be unverifiable, maximally displayable, and unadoptable on the charter’s own rules. That silence is not an omission but a requirement of the framework: a disposition installed by external requirement is a form emptied of what constitutes it, so a constitution that manufactured virtue would be performing the deprivation it exists to prevent.

Results. Sixty-one articles, thirty-six of them substantive, screened at adoption: conflict density 0.130, textual resolution 74%, runtime deferral 26%, zero unrankable pairs. Across three drafts of increasing size, density falls and textual resolution rises, by a mechanism identified as express cross-reference rather than length. Every figure is single-coder and the paper states in which direction that biases them.

title: Innovation DNA: Development and Historical Validation of a Structured Method for Forecasting the Architectural Evolution of Medical Technologies

detail.title: Innovation DNA: Development and Historical Validation of a Structured Method for Forecasting the Architectural Evolution of Medical Technologies

detail.abstract: The aim of this study was to develop a structured method for forecasting the next major architectural transition in medical technologies and to evaluate it under historically constrained information conditions. Innovation DNA separately generates an Evolutionary Vector, Forecast A (Next Realized Variant), and Forecast B (Durable Selected Branch). Following four pilot/development cases, version 2.0 was frozen and a protocol-fixed main historical series was conducted. Of 12 prespecified slots, nine underwent historical assessment and formal comparison with the subsequent technological trajectory, while three were retained as VACANT because the integrity of the historical information boundary could not be maintained. For each valid case, three separately generated structured assessments were completed before outcome disclosure. At the individual-assessment level, a full Hit was observed in 21/27 assessments for Direction (77.8%), 20/27 for the next realized variant (74.1%), and 21/26 adjudicable forecasts for the durable selected branch (80.8%); one Forecast B assessment was classified as Not yet adjudicable. In a post hoc descriptive composite, concordance across all three principal endpoints was observed in 6/9 cases (66.7%). Exploratory Full/Strong pre-outcome concordance across the three assessments was 7/9 (77.8%), 6/9 (66.7%), and 5/9 (55.6%) for Direction, Forecast A, and Forecast B, respectively. Thus, the high descriptive Hit frequency for Forecast B did not imply high reproducibility in selecting the durable branch. The findings are consistent with a predictive signal at the level of architectural direction; however, purposive case selection, within-case clustering, the absence of concurrent historical comparators, and the residual risk of latent outcome knowledge preclude claims of universal accuracy or superiority. A prospectively locked real-time validation is required to assess accuracy, reproducibility, and the incremental predictive value of Innovation DNA.

title: The SPACE™ Framework for Organizational Capacity Assessment: A Systems-Based, Equity-Centered Standard That Transforms Measurement Into Organizational Accountability

detail.title: The SPACE™ Framework for Organizational Capacity Assessment: A Systems-Based, Equity-Centered Standard That Transforms Measurement Into Organizational Accountability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Personal advancement.

detail.abstract:
Background: Philanthropic foundations and international development agencies deploy hundreds of billions of dollars annually, yet organizational failure rates remain persistently high-estimated at 15 to 30 percent-driven largely by inadequate, inconsistent, and systemically biased capacity assessment practices. This widespread measurement failure distorts resource allocation and undermines public trust. Despite a proliferation of assessment tools, including the statistically validated CCAT, Ford Foundation's OMT, McKinsey's OCAT 2.0, and over 91 instruments catalogued by the Hewlett Foundation, no universal, externally validated, equity-centered standard has achieved sector-wide adoption. This paper addresses this governance gap by proposing a standardized accountability architecture. Purpose: This paper introduces the SPACE™ Framework-a standardized, externally validated, equity-centered system for assessing organizational capacity across five interdependent domains: Strategic Alignment (S), Performance and Operations (P), Accountability and Transparency (A), Capital and Resources (C), and Empowerment and Culture (E). SPACE™ advances a central proposition: that rigorous measurement is not bureaucratic overhead but is itself a mechanism of organizational accountability-the instrument through which organizations demonstrate fidelity to mission, stewardship of resources, and authentic commitment to the communities they serve. Methods: The framework was developed through five rigorous stages: (1) systematic review and synthesis of 28 frameworks from a universe of 91-plus capacity assessment tools; (2) expert panel consultation via modified Delphi process (n = 12); (3) cognitive interview-based indicator refinement (n = 18); (4) two-phase pilot implementation across 62 organizations spanning diverse sectors, geographies, and budget sizes; and (5) full psychometric validation. The paper directly and transparently engages the most substantive critiques of standardized assessment—including the colonialism critique, the self-report bias problem, scale advantages of existing tools, and formalization bias—and provides architectural responses to each.
Findings: Psychometric validation established the framework's exceptional statistical rigor, demonstrating high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = .91; inter-rater r = .89), robust construct validity via confirmatory factor analysis (CFI = .94, TLI = .93, RMSEA = .06), and strong predictive validity for organizational performance at 24-month follow-up (r = .61 to .72). Pilot implementation further demonstrated a 75 percent reduction in assessment time and 75 to 93 percent cost reduction relative to traditional consulting approaches, alongside an 84 percent reduction in grant risk for funding decisions grounded in SPACE™ scores. Critically, blinded assessments confirmed that observed capacity score disparities between BIPOC-led and white-led organizations reflect real capacity differences driven by systemic resource inequity—not assessor prejudice—making SPACE™ a statistically reliable tool for surfacing inequity rather than encoding it.
Theoretical Contribution: SPACE™ integrates organizational systems theory, socio-technical design, signal detection theory, measurement science, behavioral economics, and network theory into a framework that repositions capacity assessment as an accountability architecture—not merely a funding gatekeeping mechanism. This contribution is especially significant for Workforce and Organizational Development scholarship, where the absence of a validated universal measurement standard has limited the field's capacity to generate cumulative, comparable knowledge about what organizational conditions produce sustained social impact.

title: Core Integrity as a Firm Characteristic: Allocation, Level, and the Limits of Public-Data Inference on Architectural Discipline

detail.abstract: Enterprise-platform doctrine holds that firms should keep the standard digital core unmodified, relocate customization to loosely coupled extensions, integrate through governed interfaces, harmonize master data, and automate operations. This paper formalizes that doctrine as an adherence-outcome framework and tests it on public data. An initial specification tested the natural theoretical refinement-that the relationship is single-peaked, with an interior optimumand returned a null alongside evidence of a measurement ceiling. Rather than stopping there, the study was re-specified to ask three questions the initial design could not address: whether adherence is a decision margin or a firm characteristic; whether the payoff lies in the allocation of adherence across dimensions rather than its level; and whether an interior optimum exists relative to each firm's own feasible maximum rather than on an absolute scale. Using a firm-year panel of 167 large US filers over 2019-2025 and the five-dimension Core Integrity Adherence Index (CIAI), I decompose adherence variance, estimate between-and within-firm associations jointly via a Mundlak specification, test allocation through dimension dispersion residualized on level, test monotonicity non-parametrically through adjusted quintile means, and test firmrelative fit through a modelled-expectation gap with an atypicality placebo. Every substantive hypothesis fails. Adherence is overwhelmingly a between-firm property (94% of variance); the primary association is negative but not significant at conventional levels and its sign is unstable across 36 defensible specifications; the inverted-U is rejected (convex, not significant); selective allocation does not outperform uniform allocation; and no dimension operates as a floor, a ceiling, or a prerequisite. Two findings survive. A Shapley decomposition shows the fivedimension composite is effectively two dimensions-data harmonization and API integration jointly carry 88% of explained variance-and both are negatively signed. Non-parametric quintile means show the highest-adherence quintile is not the best-performing, though no contrast survives multiplicity adjustment. I argue the correct reading is neither "discipline does not pay" nor "there is an inverted-U we cannot locate," but that architectural discipline is a firm characteristic whose appropriate level is firm-specific and not identifiable from pooled public data. The contribution is a corrected framework, a documented set of pre-specified failures with an explicit analysis hierarchy, and a precise statement of what instrument would be required to answer the underlying question.

detail.abstract: Predictive accuracy and decision quality can rank volatility forecasts differently because portfolio maps are invariant to some forecast errors and sensitive to others. This paper formalizes decision equivalence: statistically distinct volatility forecasts are decision-equivalent when they induce the same allocation under a specified rule. For global minimum variance, inverse-volatility, and equal-risk-contribution portfolios, common positive rescaling of marginal volatility forecasts is an exact equivalence transformation. A frozen replay on IVV, EFA, EEM, AGG, and GSG from August 2011 through July 2026 perturbs six prespecified error directions while holding correlations fixed. The common-scale placebo changes mean QLIKE by as much as 1.0024 while maximum weight deviation is 2.22e-16. The strongest cross-sectional distortion worsens QLIKE by 0.406 and raises annualized certainty-equivalent return by 4.19 percentage points, although no cell survives the frozen 120-test Holm family at 5%. Similar loss deterioration can produce zero, modest, or large portfolio-value changes, and the strongest privately useful distortion reduces cross-rule cosine similarity. A supplementary daily-return variance check on 178 complete months preserves the leading loss-deterioration signs. The results separate statistical loss, portfolio value, and allocation commonality as distinct evaluation dimensions.

detail.abstract: Nigeria's creative industry-particularly its film sector, Nollywood-represents one of the most compelling untapped economic assets on the African continent. Producing over 2,500 film titles annually, it is the world's second most prolific film industry by volume (Arewa, 2012; USITC, 2014). Yet this extraordinary creative output has not translated into proportionate economic returns, sustainable institutional growth, or meaningful international market penetration. This paper argues that the central constraint is not creative talent, financial capital, or audience demand. The constraint is structural: an absence of institutional architecture capable of absorbing investment, compounding value, and presenting a credible, governed face to the global creative market.

title: Beyond Wealth: Viable Reachability, Latent Liabilities, and Generative Continuity under Deep Uncertainty

detail.title: Beyond Wealth: Viable Reachability, Latent Liabilities, and Generative Continuity under Deep Uncertainty

detail.abstract:
Current output, asset stocks, and current productive capabilities do not necessarily identify the structure of viable transformations available to future agents. This paper develops a theoretical computational framework of Generative Continuity to formalize that gap. The framework represents present economic value jointly with a multidimensional Viable Reachability Profile, latent but physically committed liabilities, cross-domain propagation, hidden regime boundaries, endogenous knowledge, and bounded experimentation.
An analytical graph counterexample first proves that two systems can have identical current wealth, output, capability sets, and numbers of dependency links while differing in robustness and expected reconfiguration cost. Computational extensions then demonstrate the same non-equivalence under specialization, depletion, delayed harms, cross-domain spillovers, and regime shifts.
A recurrent pattern is that adaptation-path diversity and cost-adjusted accessibility can deteriorate before robustness falls and before entire options disappear. Safe adaptive learning reduces uncertainty about approach dynamics without necessarily identifying the hidden boundary itself; sufficiently isolated local experiments can recover some of that boundary information without exposing the whole system to equivalent risk.
The contribution is deliberately limited. The paper does not propose a universal monetary index of future possibility, estimate real-world frequencies from the synthetic ensembles, or introduce a new general theory of option value, viability, unawareness, or safe exploration. Its central claim is narrower: current-state economic observables do not in general identify future viable reconfigurability. This matters when future agents will face technologies, hazards, preferences, and distinctions that cannot all be represented in present decision models.

detail.abstract: Conventional climate science models the Earth's climate primarily as a chemical-thermostatic system, where greenhouse gases act as a radiative blanket modulating a static energy bucket. This paper proposes a paradigm shift: we model the Earth's climate as a thermodynamic-kinematic routing network using the operator-theoretic formalism of Loop Theory. We define the Whole (W) as the Total Planetary Thermal Energy Flow (including internal anthropogenic generation), and the Archive (A) as the Atmospheric Thermal Energy Flow (the kinematic routing state). We prove that the current climate crisis is not merely a temperature anomaly, but a forced dimensional phase transition of the Earth's Scheduler. By degrading the Decompression operator and injecting massive internal thermal loads, humanity has pushed the system off its Balance Manifold (B). This forces a collapse of the Synchronization budget and a spike in Desynchronization, manifesting physically as extreme weather. To satisfy Law 0 (Archival Completion), the Earth's Scheduler is algebraically forced to expand its dimensional footprint-breathing through Superadditive (Mode S) and Multiplicative (Mode M) regimes-risking a catastrophic trap in a Holographic (Mode H) "Venus" state. detail.abstract:
From our perspective, the digital economy functions as a seamless, modern sector dominated by service-based activities alongside the trade of goods. This study examines the evolution of India’s digital economy from the pre-1991 pre-digital era to its present-day expansion, analysing the structural transformation driven by economic liberalisation, telecommunications growth, and government-led digital initiatives.
Using a descriptive and analytical research design, this paper utilizes secondary data from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), NITI Aayog, National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), MoSPI, and international bodies such as the World Bank, IMF, and OECD. The study traces India's trajectory across four distinct phases:

* The cash-dependent pre-digital economy (pre-1991)
* The IT-led liberalisation period (1991–2000)
* The internet and mobile revolution (2000–2014)
* The accelerated digital transformation driven by the Digital India programme, Aadhaar, and the Unified Payments Interface (post-2015)

Findings show that the digital economy’s share of India's GDP rose from approximately 7.4% in 2017-18 to 11.74% in 2022-23. Concurrently, UPI transaction volumes expanded nearly 13,000-fold over a decade, internet penetration multiplied, and financial inclusion under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana scaled from near-zero to tens of crores of accounts.
Furthermore, this study evaluates the economic impact of digitalization on employment, MSMEs, agriculture, education, healthcare, and governance. It also identifies persistent challenges—such as the digital divide, cybersecurity threats, data privacy gaps, and uneven digital literacy—that continue to constrain inclusive growth. The paper concludes that while India’s digital infrastructure has scaled at a globally exceptional pace, translating this scale into equitable, welfare-enhancing outcomes remains an ongoing policy priority.
Crucially, the digital economy extends beyond online or internet-based platforms; it encompasses a vast open market operating across states and borders. It enables users to conduct real-time transactions at their convenience, 24/7, from anywhere without interruption. This contrasts sharply with the traditional economy, which typically operates on an 8-hour workday with 1.5 days of holidays per week.

title: Governing in the Gap: The EU AI Act Deferral, the Non-Life Blind Spot, and the Sixteen-Month Window for Insurance Regulators in Emerging Markets

detail.abstract: On 27 July 2026, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on Artificial Intelligence, entered into force, amending the EU Artificial Intelligence Act days before its general application date. The Regulation deferred the core Chapter III requirements for standalone high-risk AI systems under Article 6(2) and Annex III from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, a revised timetable intended to align obligations with the availability of implementation support, including harmonised standards, guidance, and conformity assessment arrangements. This paper offers an early insurance-specific analysis of the deferral and makes three contributions. First, it maps the regulatory position of insurers as at August 2026, identifying an asymmetric application phase in which transparency obligations and the Act's governance and enforcement architecture apply while the substantive Annex III high-risk regime remains deferred. Second, it examines the scope asymmetry of Annex III, which expressly identifies AI intended for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in life and health insurance, while non-life underwriting, claims triage, fraud detection, and reserving are not expressly enumerated, despite carrying much of the weight of actuarial AI deployment. Third, it asks what emerging-market insurance regulators should learn from a benchmark jurisdiction that deferred its own timetable on the eve of application. Drawing on comparative supervisory approaches in Switzerland, the United States, and Ghana, and on the author's Trust-First framework of institutionally contingent technology adoption, the paper proposes a standards-readiness sequencing model gating application dates on norm availability, supervisory capacity, and market infrastructure. The deferral, the paper argues, is not free time but a governance window.

detail.title: Leagues Are Leagues: Fixture Curation and the Unauthored Calendar in the English Premier League

detail.abstract: Leagues derive their legitimacy from calendars that are given rather than decided: everyone plays everyone twice, and the schedule falls upon all parties alike, authored by chance and constrained only by necessity. In this paper I present what I believe to be the first systematic measurement of how far the English Premier League's calendar has departed from that principle. Diffing release-day fixture lists against as-played dates across five seasons (2021/22 to 2025/26, 1,900 matches), we find that 41.4% of fixtures were played on a different date than published, whilst the composition of that movement reveals design rather than misfortune, for unplanned rescheduling collapses from 36 to 3 per season whilst deliberate broadcast movement rises from 138 to 154. Displacement and exposure are allocated by brand rather than merit: the "big six" clubs average 6.0 untelevised Saturday-3pm fixtures per season against 14.4 for all others, an allocation nearly uncorrelated with league position once those six are excluded. Against this, four market-benchmarked outcome tests (upset rates, goal totals, rest differentials and congestion overlays) return null, as results never deviate from bookmaker expectation in any kick-off slot. The costs are instead absorbed invisibly, whereby on short rest mass lineup rotation nearly doubles (29.2% against 15.3% of team-games, roughly six sigma) and the direction of squad changes inverts from restoration to downgrade. Finally, an audit of the penultimate matchweek finds the League's own stated integrity principle, that no club should play knowing what a rival has done, violated in all five seasons, 37 times, three title races included, whilst the final day remained perfectly simultaneous throughout. The Premier League enforces givenness only where it is also good television. The reform implications I propose are modest and specific.

detail.abstract: Economics increasingly recognizes that preferences, cognition, and behavior are socially embedded, yet existing approaches generally treat the different channels of social influence as analytically separate. This article proposes sympathy as a common microfoundation for the endogenous production of preferences, capabilities, and welfare. Drawing on Adam Smith's theory of sympathy and contemporary research on endogenous preferences, relational goods, and cognitive and social development, I conceptualize sympathetic synchronization as a repeated affective and cognitive process through which individuals model, respond to, and update one another. Each act of synchronization jointly produces current experienced utility, relationship-specific social capital, transferable personal human capital, and preference updating. This framework recasts the distinction between social and personal human capital as one of specificity and transferability and provides a common technology linking social interaction to preference formation and capability development. Sympathy consequently enters the model both as a developable individual capacity and as a source of experienced utility. This dual role permits an endogenous criterion of individual and social welfare based on the capacity to achieve sympathetic synchronization across increasingly diverse social and cognitive distances. The framework generates testable predictions concerning social isolation, segregation, interaction diversity, parasocial communication, and organizational investment in heterogeneous social interaction.

detail.abstract: The chapter presents Digital Calm as a neuro-behavioral model of creating sustainable emotional hospitality experiences within highly digitized settings. The digital revolution has transformed how the hospitality industry provides its services in three major aspects, which include productivity, personalization, and automation. Nonetheless, it has led to technostress, information overload, and emotional exhaustion among the customers. The combination of cognitive neuroscience, affective psychology, and service design theory makes this chapter reshape digital innovation not as a performance tool but as a tool that facilitates emotional balance and recovery. The framework has three design pillars for co-regulation, which are cognitive load regulation, affective smoothing, and autonomy-supportive design. These ideas prove that digital interfaces, AI technology, and smart services can reduce mental fatigue, in addition to the possibility of regulating the emotions of users and safeguarding their selfdetermination. Based on theory and design concepts, this chapter summarizes the latest literature in several disciplines and provides a model with the illustration of AI concierge, booking systems, and interactive guest systems in the hospitality sector. Digital Calm enhances a human-centered digital transformation by introducing neuro-behavioral principles in hospitality design to foster change.

title: Ex-Post Bilateral Fairness: Foundations for Incentives and Equilibrium in Bayesian Economies

detail.abstract: Ex-post bilateral fairness requires that the externality any agent imposes on another's payoff be reciprocated: the gain one agent confers on another must be matched by an equivalent contribution in return. This paper studies this principle as a central requirement of distributive justice for incentives and equilibrium in production environments with incomplete information. Agents hold private information (types or productivities) that determines a state-dependent technology mapping actions into output. Imposing ex-post bilateral fairness together with two intuitive principles---ex-post efficiency and inactivity---uniquely identifies an allocation rule, the ex-post fair pay (EFP), and guarantees the existence of a pure-strategy Bayesian Nash equilibrium. This identifies a novel class of Bayesian games in which pure-strategy equilibrium existence is sustained by the structure of the allocation rule rather than by standard restrictions on preferences, beliefs, or technologies. The results extend to richer environments, including formulations that incorporate more inclusive notions of fairness. Importantly, the framework yields implications for mechanism design. In a revelation mechanism that prescribes output-maximizing actions in each reported state, the EFP ensures Pareto efficiency and, under a technological monotonicity condition, delivers individual rationality and incentive compatibility. Therefore, aligning incentives with fairness can simultaneously sustain self-enforcing behavior, truthful revelation of private productivity, voluntary participation, and efficient production outcomes.

detail.abstract: We construct a firm-level text-based measure of macroeconomic perceptions from the annual reports of Chinese listed firms. The measure exhibits substantial cross-firm dispersion, with this heterogeneity systematically related to firm-and industry-level local information. Macroeconomic perceptions are more optimistic among firms with stronger own-business conditions and those in faster-growing industries, whereas regional conditions show little systematic association with these perceptions. We also find that firms whose macroeconomic perceptions are less aligned with the aggregate state exhibit greater investment inefficiency in the following year.

detail.abstract: This paper documents a systematic asymmetry in appellate outcomes between government and private appellants: while government's propensity to lauch a appealte trial are lower, they are more likily to recevie a favouralbe result in appeallate trial. Using a large sample of linked first-and second-instance judgments from 2013 to 2021, we find that government appellants are approximately 6 percentage points more likely than private appellants to obtain a favorable reversal of the firstinstance judgment. This advantage persists across a wide range of specifications, including judge fixed effects and court-by-year fixed effects. Moreover we find less evidence that this effects is driven by the political control to the court. We develop a theoretical model based on the Priest-Klein framework with repeat-player dynamics, which predicts that repeat litigants (government) will both appeal less frequently and win more conditionally-predictions that align with our empirical findings. Our results extend the literature to the economics of appellate review and suggest that repeat-player advantages operate through informational and procedural channels.

detail.abstract: Correlation neglect can induce information differentiation. In a dynamic environment with two providers, sophisticated consumers neglect correlation when updating but correctly evaluate their learning efficiency under the true information structure. They strictly prefer subscribing to both providers over subscribing to the more accurate provider alone if and only if correlation is below a cutoff we characterize. The less accurate provider can retain these consumers only when she sufficiently differentiates her information product, and the subscription cutoff serves as an equilibrium correlation cap. Whenever the cap lowers correlation, it strictly raises correlation-neglecting consumers' learning efficiency and correct-updating consumers' worst-case learning efficiency.

title:

detail.title:

detail.abstract: A meritocracy promises to allocate scarce opportunities-university places, jobs, prizes-to the most able. But ability is not observed directly; what is observed is performance, which combines talent with costly, strategically chosen effort, and effort is cheaper for the well-resourced. This paper asks whether a meritocratic system remains fair and efficient once every participant optimizes. I study competition for limited university seats through two complementary gametheoretic lenses. The first is a finite contest whose Nash equilibrium shows that competition is self-intensifying: equilibrium effort rises with the stakes, and as the field grows an ever-larger share of the prize is dissipated in effort that produces no aggregate benefit-a formal account of competitive over-investment. I compare this equilibrium to the social optimum and show that, when effort is purely positional, competition is entirely wasteful, and equilibrium welfare is only a fraction 1/N of the first best. The second lens is a large admissions market in which talent and resource-driven advantage are explicitly separated. There I show that unequal effort-costs drive a wedge between the ability bar faced by advantaged and disadvantaged applicants, so the equilibrium systematically admits weaker advantaged students over abler disadvantaged ones, and-if the gap is large enough-excludes the most disadvantaged from competing at all. I derive a closed-form index of meritocratic efficiency and show it falls as the cost gap widens, as the stakes rise, and as the system grows more selective. A welfare analysis separates genuinely productive effort from positional waste and bounds how much striving is truly lost. The central conclusion is that meritocracy is not self-stabilizing: individually rational behaviour erodes both the fairness and the efficiency that justify it. I close with the policy levers the model identifies and an explicit discussion of the equity-burnout trade-off.

title: One Gap, Three Readings: The Share-class Assumption inside the Behaviour Gap — A Reproducible Investor Return from SEC Form N-PORT, 2020–2025

detail.abstract: We compute the money-weighted return of investors in US open-end mutual funds and exchange-traded funds from SEC Form N-PORT filings, 2020 through 2025. It is 8.97 % a year, across the 7,073 funds observable through the whole window, holding 21.4 trillion dollars at its start. The flows behind it are reported fund-share transactions — mergers and partial liquidations of surviving funds included, funds of funds not netted out — so the figure prices what moved through the funds, not individual decisions. That number barely depends on the one convention the data forces on the analyst: it moves by 0.0111 percentage points across the three defensible readings. The time-weighted benchmark it is usually compared against moves by 0.68. The reason is a reporting gap. N-PORT states total returns per share class but net assets and flows only per fund, and no free structured monthly source carries net assets per share class, so the class returns cannot be weighted; the analyst has to pick one class to stand in for the fund. The behaviour gap that comes out is 0.36 percentage points under our base case, and anywhere from −0.06 to +0.62 under the three defensible picks — a spread 1.9 times the number itself: a scenario range from extreme class assumptions — not a confidence interval, and not a proven bound. 98.66 % of that movement — measured between the endpoint readings — sits on the benchmark side. Four further construction choices stay open after all the evidence is in; we publish each as a pair of readings instead of resolving it, and the base figure sits second-lowest of the seven published headline readings. On the 2,632 funds with a single share class in every month, where there is no class to pick, the gap is −0.11 percentage points — small against the construction sensitivity, and its sign is not a finding: three defensible construction choices flip it, starting with whether funds of funds are in. Our conclusion: for the full-universe headline, no defensible construction choice moves the gap as much as which share class — in substance, which fee level — the benchmark is assumed to carry: a property of the yardstick, not of the investors. And one further result. Target-date funds, built to receive automatic payroll contributions, show the largest gap of the paper's pre-specified fund groups in magnitude — and in the investors' favour, mostly in the one sharply falling year of the window. The measure reacts to how contributions meet the return path, not only to what investors decide. The dataset behind all this — 341,049 N-PORT filings across 27 quarters, 12,559 funds a month on average — is published with the code, re-downloadable without registration, its field-level pitfalls documented. Anyone can rebuild it, check it, or build something else on it.

title: MetricWorld: Measurement-consistent LiDAR-BEV Forecasting with Observation-aware Support
affiliations: Beijing Information Science and Technology University, Beijing Information Science and Technology University, Beijing Information Science and Technology University, Beijing Information Science and Technology University and Beijing Information Science and Technology University

detail.title: MetricWorld: Measurement-consistent LiDAR-BEV Forecasting with Observation-aware Support
detail.abstract:
LiDAR bird’s-eye-view (BEV) grids are derived measurement data products
used by automated-driving perception and decision systems. Their physical
interpretation is compromised when preprocessing changes grid scale or
coordinate origin between frames, or when cells without LiDAR support are
labelled as free space. This paper presents MetricWorld, a measurement-
consistent framework for short-horizon LiDAR-BEV forecasting. The
framework fixes the ego-centric region of interest, resolution, axis conven-
tion, and occupancy rule; records a two-dimensional ray-support mask; and
expresses grid quantization, scale drift, and origin drift as preprocessing-
induced measurement-error terms. A compact convolutional recurrent
network forecasts occupancy probability and nearest-return clearance at 0.3,
0.6, and 0.9 s, while unsupported target cells are excluded from supervision
and evaluation. A diagnostic moving raster produced horizontal scales of
1.751–2.780 m/cell and an origin shift of 5.363 ± 2.632 m, whereas the
proposed raster remained fixed at 0.5 m/cell. On a fixed 500-log Argoverse 2
split with 100 held-out test logs, MetricWorld reaches third-step intersection
over union of 0.6668 ± 0.0007 across three seeds. Two-way bootstrap
analysis gives third-step gains of 0.0784 over a temporal CNN, 0.0025 over
ConvLSTM, and 0.0070 over a history-only ConvGRU. Factorial ablations
show that support-masked supervision provides the largest representation
gain. The results demonstrate that fixing the measurement model and
preserving observation support improve the consistency and predictive
reliability of LiDAR-BEV data products.

title: Destroying the Doctrine of Discovery

detail.title: Destroying the Doctrine of Discovery

detail.abstract: The non-European, non-Christian world was colonized under international law that is called today the Doctrine of Discovery. This international law of colonialism was developed in the fifteenth century by Portugal, Spain, and the Catholic Church. It was thereafter adopted and adapted by England, France, and Holland in their colonial and commercial activities around the world. Under this international law, European countries claimed superior rights over Indigenous Nations and Peoples. When European explorers planted crosses and raised flags on newly discovered lands, they were making legal and religious claims of ownership, sovereignty, and conquest over the Indigenous Nations, and their lands and assets. These claims were justified on racial, ethnocentric, and religious ideas about the alleged superiority of Christian nations. This conference paper examines the application of the Doctrine around the world, and its comparative law analysis demonstrates the genocidal and pernicious effects the Doctrine created. The author identifies ten elements that comprise the Doctrine of Discovery and that demonstrate how Euro-Americans used international law to colonize Indigenous Nations. Needless to say, Euro-American domination, exploitation, and colonization seriously injured the human, property, sovereign, and self-determination rights of Indigenous Nations and Peoples, and still seriously affects them today. This conference paper sets out some initial steps that Indigenous, and non-Indigenous, peoples and nations can pursue to begin to unravel and even perhaps to destroy the international law of colonialism - the Doctrine of Discovery.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is improving on a timescale of months. The systems it will land in — power grids, tax codes, pension arrangements, international agreements, mines — move on timescales of years to decades, and those durations have not shortened over the period for which records exist. This paper argues that the principal risk of the transition is not that the technology fails but that it succeeds in the wrong order, and that the wrong order is the default rather than the exception, because nothing in the system rewards good sequencing while being first rewards whoever moves.
The argument is developed as thirty steps of plain reasoning, each stated so that a non-specialist can follow it and disagree with it. It proceeds from measured capability trends, through the displacement of high-earning cognitive work and the consequent erosion of a tax base concentrated in exactly those occupations, to the separation of productive capacity from human labour, and then to the slower systems — demography, longevity, materials, energy and expansion beyond Earth — that would have to absorb the result.
Two findings are offered for scrutiny. First, because income tax is concentrated in the most exposed occupations, fiscal damage arrives at a small fraction of the unemployment rate that institutions monitor: the signal that would raise the alarm is the signal that stays calm longest. Second, crisis does not accelerate slow institutions but routes around them, which works for money and for rules and not at all for physical infrastructure.
None of the outcomes described is harmful in itself. Each is benign if the system that absorbs it arrives first and ruinous if it does not. An appendix assembles capability rates and institutional absorption durations in commensurate units, each line sourced, so that the sequencing claim can be tested pair by pair. The observation that technology outruns institutions is long established and is known as the pacing problem; the contribution offered here is the assembly and the arithmetic rather than the insight.

title: When to Harvest: Tax-loss Harvesting as Optimal Stopping under Wash-sale Blackouts

detail.title: When to Harvest: Tax-loss Harvesting as Optimal Stopping under Wash-sale Blackouts

detail.abstract:
Most treatments of tax-loss harvesting ask how much loss a portfolio can bank and what
that loss is worth. They say little about when a given lot should be sold. Yet the timing is
itself an optimization: harvest a shallow loss today and capture a small, certain tax benefit,
or wait for a deeper loss that pays more but may never arrive, knowing that selling starts a
30-day wash-sale blackout during which the identical security cannot be repurchased without
a substitution cost. We formulate the per-lot harvest decision as an optimal-stopping problem.
The lot's log-price relative to basis follows a diffusion; stopping pays the durable tax value
of the realized loss and charges the blackout's substitution cost; the value function solves
a variational inequality with a free harvest boundary. For an arithmetic-Brownian loss we
obtain a closed-form threshold that splits cleanly into a break-even depth, equal to the
cost-to-benefit ratio, and a wait premium equal to the reciprocal of the positive root of the
characteristic equation. The formula exposes an uncomfortable fact: without mean reversion,
a patient investor should wait for implausibly deep losses (60% and beyond at plausible
volatilities), so reversion, not impatience, is what makes a finite harvest threshold sensible.
Under a mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck price the boundary is solved two independent
ways, by a projected finite-difference sweep and by a binomial dynamic program, which agree
to within a third of a percentage point of drawdown depth. The optimal once-and-done
threshold is deep, 13% to 33% of drawdown at our calibration, and rises with volatility. We
then build a model-light policy that reads the recent price path through low-order signature
features (current depth, window momentum, and realized variance recovered as the Lévy
area of the lead-lag path) and harvests when a fitted linear score crosses a cutoff. Against a
naive harvest-on-any-loss rule the signature policy adds more than 1,100% of value across
every data-generating process we test, because naive harvesting squanders a one-shot option
on the first trivial dip. Against a well-tuned static threshold it is a wash when the world
is stationary and edges ahead when volatility is stochastic and persistent, matching the
model-based boundary without needing the model.

detail.abstract: Decentralized systems such as Bitcoin (Nakamoto, 2008) typically allocate power proportionally to participants' resources. We provide an axiomatic characterization of proportional power that remains valid for all strictly increasing vNM utility functions. We introduce Small-Participant Fairness, which requires the power of each minimum-resource participant to at least equal its proportional resource share. Incentive-based Sybil Robustness rules out identity splitting that increases expected utility. Neither axiom restricts voluntary resource pooling. Together, these axioms uniquely characterize the proportional power rule. Thus, any power rule that is not proportional must either relatively disadvantage a smallest participant or permit a Sybil split that increases expected utility.

title: Does a Time-weighted Average Price Deter Settlement Manipulation? Evidence from Polymarket's Five-minute Bitcoin Markets

detail.abstract: Contracts that settle on a market price invite trading that moves the price at settlement, and the standard remedy is a time-weighted average price. Whether the average removes the incentive is rarely observed. Polymarket's five-minute bitcoin contract paid on a single Chainlink price snapshot until 7 August 2026 and on a 30-second and then a 60-second average afterwards. We measure the settlement footprint in Binance spot data at 82,752 five-minute boundaries. Under snapshot settlement the final-ten-second volume share rose from 3.05 to 5.68 percent, tenfold volume spikes became six times as frequent, and near-the-strike prices reverted. The footprint vanished in the week of the switch. Under the 60-second average the share is within 0.03 percentage points of its pre-launch level, volume did not migrate to earlier bins, and near-the-strike moves no longer revert. A one-minute average removed the footprint of a last-second push.

title: Maturity Structure and Its Impact on Option Prices
affiliations: Australian National University, RSFAS, Tsinghua University - PBC School of Finance and PBC School of Finance, Tsinghua University

detail.title: Maturity Structure and Its Impact on Option Prices
detail.abstract: We show that the maturity structure of the option market has a strong effect on option prices: a market with only monthly expirations generates predictable pricing regularities around fixed expiration days. The implied volatilities (IVs) of non-expiring options rise before and fall after the third Friday of each month, creating a monthly cycle of about 2%. Monthly demand shocks from investors' rollover activity prior to expiration, combined with supply-side frictions that limit market makers' intermediation capacity, drive this cycle. In the cross section, the magnitude of IV changes around expiration is strongly predicted by ex-ante rollover demand. Over time, the cycle becomes more pronounced during periods of elevated market risk, higher risk aversion, and tighter intermediary capital constraints. A delta-neutral straddle strategy exploiting this cycle yields returns of up to 11.3% per month. The introduction of weekly options weakens the IV cycle, consistent with reduced rollover demand.

title: Measuring the Physical Scale of the Economy: Why Material Footprints Remain Essential for Sustainability Assessment

detail.title: Measuring the Physical Scale of the Economy: Why Material Footprints Remain Essential for Sustainability Assessment
detail.abstract: Mathis Wackernagel’s critique of material footprint accounting is timely. Material footprints have moved from a specialist tool of industrial ecology into the Sustainable Development Goals, international resource assessments, national statistical systems, and, increasingly, circular-economy and resource-use targets. This growing policy significance makes questions of scientific legitimacy, indicator interpretation, and the distinction between empirical measurement and normative target-setting increasingly consequential. Wackernagel identifies five fundamental limitations: an unclear research question, arbitrary exclusions, aggregation without biophysical equivalence, the absence of an intrinsic upper limit, and normative thresholds presented as scientifically derived. We agree that material footprints should not be interpreted as direct measures of environmental impact and that absolute resource-use targets cannot be derived mechanically from aggregate tonnes. However, we reject the conclusion that these characteristics constitute fundamental scientific weaknesses. The critique applies the requirements of an environmental impact or sustainability indicator to a physical accounting system with a different purpose. Economy-wide material flow accounting measures the physical scale and structure of socioeconomic metabolism and complements the monetary System of National Accounts by quantifying natural-resource flows associated with production, trade and final demand. Aggregation by mass establishes physical magnitude, not environmental equivalence, while material composition and complementary environmental accounts enable assessment of differentiated pressures and impacts. Material footprints extend this framework by attributing upstream extraction through global supply chains to final demand. Their growing policy relevance therefore calls for clearer separation between physical accounting, environmental impact assessment and sustainability target-setting.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) on the energy efficiency of participating countries, using the data from 149 countries between 1995 and 2023. Based on the energy efficiency estimated by the stochastic frontier approach (SFA), we assess the treatment effect of the BRI through the staggered DID and event study approach. We find that the BRI improved involved countries' energy efficiency by 1.9 percentage points; as the increase of participating years, the positive effects are statistically more significant and more salient in magnitude. Our results remain robust across a battery of robustness checks, including sensitivity analysis of parallel trend, heterogeneity treatment assessments, PSM-DID, ruling out alternative explanations, and so on. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the positive treatment effect is significant for high-income countries, Asia-Pacific and European countries, and countries with high energy endowments. Further analysis over potential mechanisms yields that the impact is channeled through renewable energy transition and enhanced energy efficiency governance. These findings confirm the contribution of China's BRI in achieving the global goal of carbon neutrality and shed light on the path of related countries' further sustainable development in practice.

detail.abstract: This work explores an unexpected byproduct of land reform in 1950s Italy, a rise in female labor force participation (FLFP). Using difference-indifferences methods I show that areas experiencing land reform saw a rise in the share of women working outside the home. To control for potential endogeneity, the location of Imperial Roman colonies is introduced as a new instrument for pre-reform landholding inequalities. The work shows how the land reform affected agricultural knowledge, land property rights, and rural infrastructure, changing the agricultural sector. The work then details the mechanisms through which these changes in the agricultural sector increased FLFP.

detail.abstract: How do crop-specific drought shocks affect agricultural production and subsequent crop allocation? We combine Mexican agricultural records with municipal drought maps and construct exposure from the historical location of each crop within a state and agricultural cycle. Drought operates primarily through physical quantities: one additional exposure point reduces production volume by 11.1% and production value by 11.6%. Crop groups with negative and statistically significant contemporaneous volume responses experience larger realized losses; for these empirically sensitive groups, a onestandard-deviation shock lowers realized gross revenue per sown hectare by about 10%, almost entirely through lower physical output; farmgate prices provide essentially no compensation. These groups subsequently follow a weaker sown-area path relative to other crop groups. This divergence is consistent with a drought-induced change in crop composition, without implying hectare-by-hectare switching or a contraction in aggregate agricultural land.

title: Profit Erosion and Sequential Merger Dynamics

detail.title: Profit Erosion and Sequential Merger Dynamics
detail.abstract: Sequential merger dynamics are immediate in two polar cases. Under homogeneous-productBertrand competition, equilibrium profits vanish whenever more than one firm remains, creatingthe strongest possible incentive toward monopolization. At the opposite extreme, when firmsproduce independent goods and there are no technological interactions across firms, individualprofits do not depend on the number of active firms and mergers create no private surplus. Mostindustries lie between these extremes. This paper argues that the relevant primitive for mergerdynamics is therefore the industry’s profit erosion profile: the sequence of individual equilibriumprofits as the number of independent firms varies.We develop a recursive solution method for sequential merger games with an arbitrary profiterosion profile. At each state, seller indifference determines explicitly the acquisition offer compatiblewith any candidate acceptance probability. The buyer’s equilibrium problem is consequentlyreduced to a one-dimensional maximization, irrespective of the number of firms. Therecursive formulation identifies three qualitatively distinct merger regimes—the status quo, aninterior war of attrition, and immediate acquisition—and relates transitions among them tothe erosion of individual profits as market fragmentation increases. Linear Cournot and Salopcompetition provide contrasting benchmarks, while the family πm = (m + 1)−n is used as alaboratory for varying profit erosion continuously. The four-firm case illustrates the recursivecompression of lower-state equilibria and yields an analytical boundary between the status quoand active merger behavior.1

detail.title: Managing Existential Risk from AI: Investing in Delay, Learning and Alignment

detail.abstract: We study the potential arrival of artificial general super-intelligence (AI) as an existential risk management problem for humanity. Policymakers have proposed delaying AI, learning about risks from AI, and investing in AI alignment, but these policies are typically evaluated in isolation. We develop an integrated model in which AI arrival is uncertain and irreversible, and safety investments affect both timing and the likelihood of adverse outcomes. The value of delay is determined by expected improvements over time in AI alignment and-in the presence of impatience-the expected net benefit of AI arrival. The value of delay informs optimal investment in delay and its interaction with investments in alignment and in learning about the value of delay. Depending on model parameters, investments in alignment can either crowd in or crowd out investments in delay. Learning can affect investments in delay in non-monotonic ways. We use this framework to map different sets of beliefs about risks from AI and the efficacy of safety technologies into policy preferences.

detail.abstract: We study whether investor voice can help address global externalities under fragmented regulation. In our setting, a multinational firm generates externalities across jurisdictions, national regulators face political frictions that can impede corrective regulation, and policy differences create scope for regulatory arbitrage and production leakage. We compare two channels of investor influence: corporate stewardship, which affects firms' global operations, and policy advocacy, which affects local regulation. Both channels can help address global externalities, but their relative effectiveness depends on political frictions abroad. When these frictions are severe enough to prevent foreign regulation, leakage weakens policy advocacy but strengthens stewardship. When foreign regulation is politically feasible, however, stewardship can crowd out foreign regulation and reinforce policy miscoordination, while local policy advocacy can crowd in foreign regulation and reduce externalities abroad.

detail.abstract: Leveraging Texas household data from 2005 to 2022, I determine evidence of regional regulatory capture in Texas panhandle electric utility operation. Deriving a rational choice variation of soft capture, the model under modest assumptions predicts an increased incentive for rent seeking behavior from electric utilities operating with jurisdiction over smaller residential populations due to larger potential gains against legislators under incomplete cost information. Exploiting a 2010 acquisition of electrical transmission assets in Lubbock, Texas by Lubbock Power and Light as a candidate for the predicted selection, I employ multiple difference-indifferences specifications and estimate reduced-form evidence of anticipated increases in consumer electric billing in excess of acquisition costs. Under conservative assumptions with the preferred specification, the permitted regulatory shift in Lubbock in 2010 increased aggregate annual electric utility costs for residential consumers in Lubbock by an estimated $14,834,879 annually for customers of LP&L alone, or $192,853,420 from 2010 to 2022. Results provide additional evidence of vulnerability in cost-of-service regulatory policy implementations without performance-based regulatory components.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a monthly Political Capital Index (PCI) that transforms the multidimensional U.S. political landscape into a continuous measure of an administration’s capacity to implement its policy agenda. The PCI integrates four theoretically motivated dimensions: electoral mandate, House strength, Senate strength, and presidential-tenure capital. Across 957 months from 1945–2024, the PCI takes 957 distinct values, capturing political variation obscured by discrete regime classifications. External validation shows that seniority capital is positively associated with presidential approval, while subsequent legislative production provides criterion-based validation of the composite index. Higher PCI is associated with lower realized equity-market volatility across aggregate, size, and industry portfolios, but does not systematically predict excess returns. Although average PCI differs historically across presidential parties, the PCI–volatility association does not differ significantly by party. Overall, PCI provides a theoretically grounded, empirically validated, party-neutral framework for translating political climate into financial risk.

title: The Algebraic Collapse of the Efficiency Benchmark and the Inherited Impossibility of the Social Welfare Function: Structural Complexity, Representational Limits, and the Geometry of the Economic Design Space

detail.title: The Algebraic Collapse of the Efficiency Benchmark and the Inherited Impossibility of the Social Welfare Function: Structural Complexity, Representational Limits, and the Geometry of the Economic Design Space

declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Allocative efficiency requires a stable cost-based ordering of governance arrangements. We demonstrate that such an ordering becomes mathematically impossible when transactions are interdependent. In the paper, we model governance decision-making as an iterative design process under bounded rationality, formalized as a dimensional constraint on actors' representational capacity. Central to this framework is the design space: a stratified mixed domain combining discrete structural boundaries with continuous intensive margins. This reflects economic reality: discrete organizational and institutional thresholds impose boundaries, while continuous margins permit smooth adjustment (e.g., monitoring intensity). Actors generate candidate governance designs, evaluate risks, and translate them into costs via a lower-dimensional, capacity-constrained projection of the design space. 

We prove an impossibility theorem: under structural complexity, interdependencies deform the design space's causal architecture and invalidate the domain stability required for a well-defined cost metric. The risk-to-cost mapping breaks down, rendering efficiency rankings indeterminate. Fallback heuristics cannot restore a coherent metric and trade-offs cannot be evaluated in efficiency terms. This indeterminacy is structural: in a deformed design space, even an unbounded actor cannot construct a well-defined cost metric. The social welfare function inherits this collapse and ceases to exist as a well-defined mathematical object. In such environments, markets do not "fail" to reach an efficient equilibrium; they operate in a space where efficiency is no longer a mathematically meaningful property. Consequently, this framework shifts the macro conversation away from market failures to a deeper insight: markets can allocate neither efficiently nor inefficiently when efficiency cannot be ranked.

detail.abstract: Readers learn not only from a media source but also how to read it. We ask how this source-specific interpretive capital is priced when subscribers renew and whether transparency that travels across sources differs from feedback attached to past consumption. In a Gaussian model, familiarity raises the value of future reports at a diminishing rate and matters most at intermediate source expertise. Conditional on an inherited one-sided consumption history and terminal or myopic pricing, the better-understood source charges more, retains more of its returning cohort, and earns more from it. Symmetric public calibration and consumption-linked outcome feedback both improve consumer decisions but move competition in opposite directions. Calibration helps the unfamiliar source more and compresses the report-value advantage; feedback deepens understanding only of consumed content and expands it. Within the covered interior market and before implementation costs, feedback also raises gross renewal-period surplus. Public calibration may lower it only in a strongly concentrated returning cohort—where the familiar source initially serves more than four fifths—because readers are reallocated away from a source that remains more informative. What matters, therefore, is not simply how much transparency is produced, but whether it is portable across sources.

keywords: Prewar and Postwar U.S. Time Series

detail.abstract: It is well established that the U.S. prewar output was more volatile and less shockpersistent than the postwar output. This is often attributed to the data interpolation employed to construct the prewar series, rather than the postwar stabilization policies and institutional changes. Our analytical results, however, indicate that commonly used linear interpolation has the opposite effect on shock persistence and volatility of a series-it reduces short-run volatility and raises shock persistence. Therefore, interpolation does not seem to explain away the observed gaps between the volatility and shock persistence of the prewar and postwar series. If anything, it may hide part of the true gap. Consequently, our results strengthen the case that the prewar-postwar difference reflects real economic changes rather than interpolation, leaving stabilization policies and institutional changes as possible explanations. Our results hold for parsimonious stationary and nonstationary time series commonly used to model macroeconomic data. Our theoretical finding is also supported by a counterfactual empirical exercise we conduct using U.S. postwar series.

title: Oil, Derivation, and the Politics of Fiscal Federalism in Nigeria: Why the 13% Consensus Holds, and Why It Cannot Hold

detail.abstract: The derivation principle, which returns a share of natural-resource revenue to the state where it is produced, has been the most persistently contested feature of Nigerian fiscal federalism since the return to civilian rule in 1999. Section 162(2) of the Constitution sets it at not less than 13 per cent, a figure that has held for over two decades despite near-universal elite dissatisfaction. This article asks how thirteen per cent became a political floor rather than a principled settlement, and why it both endures and provokes mounting demands for change. Drawing on 167 elite interviews conducted across Nigeria's six geo-political zones in 2017, read alongside the constitutional history of resource revenue from the fifty per cent of the independence constitutions to the present, it shows that the floor rests on a coalition of three resistance logics, structural-arithmetic, constitutional-ownership and governance-sufficiency, set against three distinct demand-side arguments. It introduces and tests a fiscal proxy theory of restructuring, which reads constitutional demands as redistributive ones in disguise, and finds it powerful but incomplete. The article argues that the floor is unlikely to hold as oil revenue declines, and that a derivation principle extended to all mineral producers offers the most politically viable route to reform.

detail.abstract: We examine long-run educational outcomes across the territories classified under Kazakhstan's 1992 radiation-risk zoning around the Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site using individual-level data from the national university entrance examination for the 2021-2023 graduating cohorts. Students in the highest-risk designated territories, Zones 1 and 2, score 0.17-0.21 standard deviations lower on the examination and are around 15 percentage points less likely to receive a merit-based university scholarship than comparable students in neighbouring non-designated rural areas. The neighbouring Zone 3, which received a comparable radiation-risk designation, exhibits no such disadvantage. The Zones 1 and 2 penalty persists for most outcomes after accounting for reconstructed radiation exposure and is not explained by pre-designation educational differences or observable school characteristics. Instead, it is concentrated in a predominantly rural territory that experienced severe and persistent post-Soviet demographic decline. The findings suggest that long-run educational differences across designated territories depend not only on historical exposure but also on the demographic and economic trajectories of the territories to which the designations were attached.

detail.abstract: Global games select a unique cutoff when a player's incentive moves monotonically with private information. We show that this logic can fail when a privately informed participant can take a costly, simultaneous, and unobserved action that defends the status quo. In a currency-attack model, the defender acts only at intermediate signals. Along the traders' cutoff equation, this interval response creates an endogenous defense-loss term that vanishes at the endpoints of an activation component but can dominate the decreasing benchmark payoff margin in between. We establish a primitive region in which defense is inactive and uniqueness survives, and a finite-CDF overshoot condition under which two active-defense cutoff roots coexist with the inactive benchmark root. Because marginal indifference need not imply global incentives, we also give sufficient conditions for a genuine monotone cutoff best response. Finally, outward-rounded interval arithmetic proves that a proper-prior parameter vector has exactly three symmetric monotone-cutoff equilibria and that this topology persists locally. The result isolates a payoff-based boundary of global-game selection: hidden intervention can restore multiplicity without public signalling or a perturbation of the information hierarchy.

detail.abstract: This study examines EPC Band C threshold status and subsequent recorded EPC-score changes in high-floor residential buildings in England and Wales (2013-2023), using Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) data. A previously unreported panel-construction problem, Unique Property Reference Numbers are occasionally recorded at a building rather than unit level, is identified and addressed using a conservative same-unit filtering procedure. A threshold-based eligibility construction is shown to be mechanically related to recorded EPC improvement when measured from a dwelling's post-improvement rather than baseline score: this timing choice alone accounts for the entire positive association found in a naive baseline specification. Measured instead from the baseline score, the association reverses its sign under every panel-construction and threshold combination tested, a reversal corroborated by a regression discontinuity design using a different estimation strategy on the same score variable, though the estimated magnitude is sensitive to bandwidth choice. Two secondary strategies examining whether interest rates moderate this relationship produced no credible estimates, so this question remains open. The findings indicate that eligibility indicators built from the same data used to measure outcomes require explicit attention to measurement timing, with implications for evaluations using EPC thresholds as proxies for financial or policy eligibility.

detail.abstract: We examined the relationship between agricultural credit intensity and rice productivity across the ten highest rice-producing states in India by rice production in 2020-21. We use official state-level measures of rice yield, irrigation coverage, agricultural credit, and total cropped area. Credit intensity is defined as cumulative agricultural ground-level credit disbursement reported through December 2020 per hectare of total cropped area. Because the credit series covers agriculture and allied activities rather than rice alone, it is interpreted as an indicator of the broader state agricultural-finance environment. The descriptive results show a positive cross-state association, the Pearson correlation is 0.475, and the baseline regression coefficient is 0.00466 kg/ha per rupee of credit intensity (p = 0.165, R 2 = 0.226). The analysis is descriptive rather than causal, and the estimated relationship is interpreted in the context of other conditions affecting rice production, including irrigation, input access, and financial infrastructure.

title: Binary correlation as a goodness-of-fit measure for a binomial logit model: the Pearson-Matthews-Cramer connection
